schemes.name: Floyd Nolen Jones
schemes.summary: A conservative Masoretic chronology that treats the Genesis 5 and 11 genealogies as continuous, with no gaps between father and son. It is the scheme the underlying event timeline was compiled under, so it is the only one here with a date for every event.
schemes.source: Floyd Nolen Jones, The Chronology of the Old Testament, via Theographic Bible Metadata

schemes.name: James Ussher (1650)
schemes.summary: The most famous biblical chronology, published in the Annals of the World and printed in the margins of many King James Bibles. Ussher placed the first day of creation on 23 October 4004 BC. Like Jones he reads the genealogies as continuous; the two differ by only a year or two at most points.
schemes.source: James Ussher, Annals of the World (1650, English 1658)

schemes.name: Septuagint (LXX) reckoning
schemes.summary: The Greek Old Testament gives different ages in the patriarchal genealogies and inserts an extra ancestor after the flood, producing a far longer span - roughly 4,777 years from creation to the completion of the Second Temple. Early Christian writers such as Eusebius worked from these figures. No per-event dates are loaded for this scheme.
schemes.source: Chronology of the Bible (overview of textual traditions)

schemes.name: Samaritan Pentateuch reckoning
schemes.summary: The Samaritan Pentateuch gives yet another set of genealogical figures, yielding roughly 3,000 years from creation to the settlement of Canaan. It is the shortest of the three textual traditions. No per-event dates are loaded for this scheme.
schemes.source: Chronology of the Bible (overview of textual traditions)

schemes.name: Edwin R. Thiele
schemes.summary: Not a chronology of the whole Bible but of the Hebrew monarchy, and the usual starting point for scholarly work on it. Thiele worked inductively from how ancient scribes actually counted regnal years: Judah used accession-year reckoning and Israel non-accession, Israel's year began in spring and Judah's in autumn, and co-regencies overlap. That resolves most of the apparent contradictions in Kings. Later scholars corrected him on points such as Hezekiah's co-regency with Ahaz.
schemes.source: Edwin R. Thiele, The Mysterious Numbers of the Hebrew Kings

schemes.name: Mainstream critical
schemes.summary: Rather than counting genealogies, this approach anchors the biblical narrative to dates fixed by Assyrian, Babylonian and Egyptian records and by archaeology. It offers no date for creation at all, treats the primeval history as outside the reach of chronology, and becomes confident only from the divided monarchy onward.
schemes.source: Standard reference works on ancient Near Eastern chronology

notes.heading: Why the dates differ
notes.body:
There is no single biblical chronology, and any app that shows you one date without saying whose it is has made a choice on your behalf.

The disagreements come from three places. First, the manuscript traditions differ: the Hebrew Masoretic Text, the Greek Septuagint and the Samaritan Pentateuch give different ages in the genealogies of Genesis 5 and 11, and the Septuagint adds an ancestor after the flood. Those differences alone move creation by well over a thousand years.

Second, chronologists disagree about whether the genealogies are continuous. Read as an unbroken father-to-son chain, they yield a creation around 4000 BC. Read as a selective list that skips generations - a normal practice in ancient genealogy - they yield no total at all.

Third, the regnal records in Kings and Chronicles are genuinely hard. Reigns are counted differently in Israel and Judah, co-regencies overlap, and the two books sometimes disagree. Reconciling them is the problem Edwin Thiele spent a career on.

notes.heading: What is actually fixed
notes.body:
Not everything is contested. From the divided monarchy onward, the biblical narrative can be tied to Assyrian and Babylonian records that carry their own dates, and the agreement is broadly good.

The later the event, the firmer the ground. The fall of Jerusalem to Babylon and the edict of Cyrus permitting the return are fixed within a year or two by external sources, and essentially every scheme agrees about them. The uncertainty is concentrated in the primeval history and the patriarchs, where there is nothing outside the text to check against.

notes.heading: Why some schemes show no date
notes.body:
The event timeline in this app was compiled under one scheme, Floyd Nolen Jones's, so that is the only one with a date for all 450 events. Other schemes carry only the dates that can be traced to a published statement of that chronology.

Where a scheme has no date for an event, the app says so. It does not quietly fall back to another scheme's number and present it as that scheme's answer. A blank is information.

notes.heading: Which should you use
notes.body:
If you want the chronology printed in the margins of a King James Bible, choose Ussher. If you want a modern conservative reckoning of the same kind, Jones is the default here and differs from Ussher by only a year or two at most points.

If you are reading alongside academic commentary, the critical scheme will match what you find there, at the cost of offering no dates for the earliest chapters. None of these is the app's opinion. The choice is yours and you can change it at any time.
